criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale - Include the following required information: • What is the spacecraft's primary mission? • Why is the mission needed? • How many spacecraft are used and why? • Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: Mission purpose, single-satellite rationale, and users (operator, customers, funding) are addressed with context and cited literature. Operator is somewhat vague (university or government) and users are not firmly named as operator versus customer, so it falls just short of top marks.

evidence.quote: Coral reefs harbour some of the most diverse species of life on the planet
The proposed satellite would likely be used by governmental and science agencies (e.g. CSIRO, BOM) for research and/or education.

criteria.name: Main body: mission design - Present a summary of the mission design using software and/or hand calculations as appropriate - Include relevant screenshots and software files (in the main body of the report and/or appendix) - Include the following information: • Where it will launch from, and using which launch vehicle? Why did you choose this option? • What type of orbit will you use? What are its characteristics and orbital elements? • Will you need to perform any orbital maneuvers? • Which ground control facilities will you use? • How often will your spacecraft be able to communicate with ground control? • How long will the mission last, and what are your plans for EOL?
criteria.reasoning: Covers launch, orbit, ground station and EOL with STK screenshots and an access table. However, the Vega E is not yet built and the launch site reasoning is muddled (Kourou latitude vs target inclination). The RAAN of 27.33° is unexplained, the Vega E/piggyback choice is inconsistent, the orbit is described as both retrograde and sun-synchronous without justification, the 600 km altitude rationale is weak, and manoeuvre/EOL analysis is incomplete with an unfinished drag-sail sentence. STK files are not evidently attached.

evidence.quote: Specifically, an altitude of 600km requires a mean inclination of $ 97.7924^{\circ} $ for the satellite to remain sun-synchronous.
The orbit is near-polar and retrograde, meaning the satellite will pass over almost the entire Earth
The proposed satellite will thus use the Vega E rocket as a launch vehicle

criteria.name: Conclusion
criteria.reasoning: Conclusion summarises the segments and notes launch risk and alternatives, but it is largely a restatement and does not draw quantitative conclusions from the access data or perturbation results.

evidence.quote: A specific launch vehicle – the Vega E – has been selected although it has not been built yet.

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: Clear headings and a sensible structure, but there are unfinished sentences, a broken drag-sail sentence, a broken reference [10], a contents page not matching sections, and reliance on Wikipedia [6], which the brief prohibits. Table and figure labelling is inconsistent, with no figure numbers or titles, and some grammar errors.

evidence.quote: The ZYZZsat is small and without thrusters in a low-earth orbit.

technical_issues.issue: Vega E is planned but not built; the piggyback alternative (Vega/SSMS) and the choice of Vega E are inconsistent, and the 2024 first flight claim is unsupported.
Argument that equatorial launch and a 5.05°N site are relevant to a 97.8° orbit is muddled; launch windows reasoning is incorrect as stated.
Describes orbit as both retrograde and sun-synchronous without explaining inclination gives retrograde motion; RAAN of 27.33° is unexplained.
Argument of latitude is described as 'angle from ascending node', correct, but the table states u=0° as a fixed value while text says it changes; inconsistent.
Claims polar ground stations maximise passes but then states a Tasmanian site; mean contact of ~10 min is not checked against elevation mask; access table lists duplicate row 14 and 15.
Uncontrolled re-entry argued as least energy but the drag sail sentence is truncated; graveyard option is wrongly stated as applicable only to GEO and no delta-v is calculated.

overall: A reasonably structured report with a clear mission concept and STK evidence, but significant gaps: unresolved launch vehicle choice, unexplained orbital elements, incomplete EOL analysis, truncated sentences, missing figure numbering and a prohibited Wikipedia source. Overall a mid-range Adequate submission.

feedback.summary: You have a clear mission concept, with a well-supported case for a single satellite and a sensible report structure, and your STK evidence gives the design a solid base. The main gaps are an unresolved launch vehicle choice, unexplained orbital elements, an incomplete end-of-life analysis, and several broken or unfinished sentences and references. Fixing these would move the report up a band.
next_steps: Resolve the launch vehicle: choose one option, justify it against your target orbit, and remove the conflicting Vega E and piggyback statements. Check the 2024 first-flight claim against a source.

Explain your orbital elements in the text: why the inclination gives retrograde motion, what sun-synchronous means here, and how the RAAN of 27.33° was chosen. Make the argument of latitude consistent between text and table.

Complete the end-of-life section: finish the drag-sail sentence, calculate the delta-v for any manoeuvre you propose, and replace the Wikipedia source with an approved reference. Also fix the duplicate rows 14 and 15 in the access table and attach your STK files.

criteria.C1: You clearly state the primary mission, the reason it is needed and why one spacecraft is used, supported by cited literature on coral reef monitoring. To reach the top band, name the operator and customers separately and explain each role. Give more specific detail on who would use the data and how.
criteria.C2: Your STK screenshots and access table show a solid design process. To reach the top band, the design must be consistent and fully justified. Explain the launch site and vehicle choice in terms of your target inclination, justify the orbit and its elements, and check your ground station contact times against an elevation mask. Complete the manoeuvre and end-of-life analysis with calculated delta-v and attach the software files.
criteria.C3: Your conclusion summarises the mission segments and identifies the launch risk and alternatives, which is useful. To reach the top band, draw specific conclusions from your evidence. Refer to the access durations, contact times and perturbation results, and state what they mean for the mission's feasibility.
criteria.C4: The report has clear headings and a logical structure. To improve, finish the unfinished sentences and fix the broken reference [10]. Use approved sources instead of Wikipedia. Number and title every figure and table, and check the contents page against the section headings. Proofread for grammar and keep the language formal throughout.
